A.explanation: Horizontal velocity $V \cos \theta$ is constant because there is no horizontal acceleration, so $R = (V \cos \theta)T$.

B.explanation: $V \sin \theta$ is the initial vertical component of velocity, not the horizontal component, so it cannot give the horizontal range $R$.

C.explanation: The term $-\frac{1}{2}gT^2$ describes vertical acceleration due to gravity and has no effect on horizontal motion when air resistance is negligible.

D.explanation: This is the form of the vertical displacement equation using $V \sin \theta$, not the horizontal displacement $R$.

hints: Notice that $R$ in the diagram is measured purely along the horizontal dashed line from P to Q.
Recall that the launch velocity $V$ at angle $\theta$ splits into horizontal $V \cos \theta$ and vertical $V \sin \theta$ components.
Think about which direction has zero acceleration when air resistance is negligible and gravity $g$ acts vertically downward.
walkthrough: Identify the useful information: $R$ is horizontal displacement, $T$ is total time of flight, and launch velocity $V$ is at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.
State the physical rule: with negligible air resistance, horizontal acceleration is zero while vertical acceleration is $-g$, so horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
Resolve the initial velocity: horizontal component is $V_x = V \cos \theta$ and vertical component is $V_y = V \sin \theta$.
Set up horizontal motion with constant velocity: $s_x = V_x T$ because the $\frac{1}{2}a_xT^2$ term is zero.
Substitute $s_x = R$ and $V_x = V \cos \theta$ to get $R = VT \cos \theta$ with no $gT^2$ term. This is option A.
